title: Neonatal Bacterial Meningitis - Merck Manual Professional Edition

claims.text: The predominant pathogens of neonatal bacterial meningitis are Group B streptococcus (GBS), Escherichia coli (especially K1-polysaccharide strains), and Listeria monocytogenes.
claims.byte_quote: The **predominant pathogens** are the following: [Group B streptococcus](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/streptococcal-infections) (GBS) [_Escherichia coli_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-negative-bacilli/escherichia-coli-infections) (particularly those strains containing the K1 polysaccharide) [_Listeria monocytogenes_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-bacilli/listeriosis)

claims.text: Other reported pathogens include enterococci, nonenterococcal group D streptococci, alpha-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, gram-negative enteric organisms (Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter diversus), Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
claims.byte_quote: **Other reported pathogens** include [enterococci](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/enterococcal-infections), nonenterococcal group D streptococci, [alpha-hemolytic streptococci](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/streptococcal-infections), [_Staphylococcus aureus_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/staphylococcal-infections), [coagulase-negative staphylococci](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/staphylococcal-infections), gram-negative enteric organisms (eg, [_Klebsiella_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-negative-bacilli/klebsiella-enterobacter-and-serratia-infections) species, [_Enterobacter_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-negative-bacilli/klebsiella-enterobacter-and-serratia-infections) species, _Citrobacter diversus_), [_Haemophilus influenzae_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-negative-bacilli/haemophilus-infections), [_Neisseria meningitidis_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-negative-cocci-and-coccobacilli/meningococcal-diseases), and [_Streptococcus pneumoniae_](/professional/infectious-diseases/gram-positive-cocci/streptococcal-infections).

claims.text: Incidence is 3/10,000 in full-term neonates and 1/1,000 in low-birth-weight neonates, so low birth weight is a host risk factor.
claims.byte_quote: Neonatal bacterial meningitis occurs in 3/10,000 full-term and in 1/1,000 low-birth-weight (LBW) neonates

claims.text: Neonatal bacterial meningitis most often results from the bacteremia of neonatal sepsis, with higher blood-culture colony counts conferring higher meningitis risk.
claims.byte_quote: Neonatal bacterial meningitis most frequently results from the bacteremia that occurs with neonatal sepsis; the higher the colony count in the blood culture, the higher the risk of meningitis.

claims.text: Scalp lesions are a route of infection, particularly developmental defects creating communication between the skin surface and the subarachnoid space.
claims.byte_quote: Neonatal bacterial meningitis may also result from scalp lesions, particularly when developmental defects lead to communication between the skin surface and the subarachnoid space

claims.text: Definitive diagnosis is made by CSF examination via lumbar puncture in any neonate suspected of sepsis or meningitis; no Gram-stain organism morphology is described on this page.
claims.byte_quote: Definitive diagnosis of neonatal bacterial meningitis is made by CSF examination. Lumbar puncture (LP), which should be performed in any neonate suspected of having sepsis or meningitis.
